# 4 Maccabees Chapter 2 — The EMET Bible (Literal)
**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Reason's Rule Over the Passions

---

**2:1** Now if reason rules over the passions that impede one from justice — namely greed and desire — it is also clear that it rules over the passions that hinder one from courage, namely anger, pain, and fear.

**2:2** How is it that reason masters love of money? When a person cleaves to the law, even if a lover of money, he is compelled by the law to lend without interest to the needy and to cancel the debt at the jubilee.

**2:3** If one is greedy, reason masters his greed by the law so that he does not glean his fields or harvest every grape from his vineyard — and in all other matters one may observe this principle mastering the passions.

**2:4** For the law prevails even over affection for parents, so that virtue is not surrendered for their sake.

**2:5** It prevails over love for one's wife, so that one rebukes her when she transgresses.

**2:6** It takes precedence over love for children, so that one punishes them for their vices.

**2:7** It prevails over the ties of friendship, so that one reproves friends when they act wickedly.

**2:8** And do not think it strange that reason, through the law, is able to master even enmity — in that it forbids cutting down the cultivated trees of enemies and protects the property of enemies from destroyers.

**2:9** And it masters the more violent emotions too: lust for power, vanity, boasting, arrogance, and malice.

**2:10** For the temperate mind repels all these malicious emotions, just as it repels anger — for it masters even that.

**2:11** Indeed when Moses was angry with Dathan and Abiram, he did nothing against them in anger, but governed his anger by reason.

**2:12** For the temperate mind, as I said, is able to get the better of the passions, and to redirect some and to destroy the power of others.

**2:13** Why else did the wise Jacob rebuke the households of Simeon and Levi for their irrational slaughter of the whole tribe of the Shechemites, saying, 'Cursed be their anger'?

**2:14** For if reason did not have the power to restrain anger, he would not have said this.

**2:15** For at the time when God fashioned man, he planted within him his emotions and his moral character.

**2:16** At that time he also enthroned upon the senses the mind as the sacred governor over all these.

**2:17** And to the mind he gave the law, and one who lives subject to the law will rule over a kingdom that is temperate and just and good and courageous.

**2:18** How then, one might ask, if reason is master of the passions, is it not master of forgetfulness and ignorance?

**2:19** The argument is absurd. For reason is not sovereign over its own weaknesses, but over the passions that are opposed to justice, courage, temperance, and prudence — and over those it is sovereign, not in such a way as to destroy them, but so as not to yield to them.

**2:20** I could prove to you from many and various examples that reason is indeed sovereign over the passions.

**2:21** Fire blazes most fiercely, but it is quickly extinguished by water; so also passion, though it burns intensely, is quenched by the rational mind.

**2:22** One may perceive this in many instances, but most clearly in the deeds of Eleazar.

**2:23** For when Eleazar was in the midst of being tortured — with the fire still blazing, with his blood still flowing — he withstood that terrible ordeal of pain.
